title: Ukraine’s Defense Industry — The Motor of Post-War Revival
content:
Defense production capacity in Ukraine is projected to hit $55bn this year, according to the National Security and Defense Council in Kyiv, compared to $1bn before 2022’s full-scale invasion. That’s close to a quarter of national GDP.

Given the need to stay heavily armed even if Russia agrees to a ceasefire, and given the global interest in Ukrainian weaponry, the industry is likely to dominate economic reconstruction. Arms and the technology now embedded inside them could play as big a part in the industry as they do in another “porcupine” country, Israel.

More than four years of war, in which low-cost drones, interceptors, and missiles have been developed, tested, and honed on the battlefield, have resulted in unparalleled technological advances. And Ukraine can expect to leverage them for a hefty markup when exported to the West, the Middle East, and elsewhere.

The shape of a defense-led recovery depends on whether Ukraine makes the right deals in Europe as it seeks to maximize the value of its expertise, according to Tamar Jacoby, director of the Progressive Policy Institute’s New Ukraine Project.

title: Ukraine: Fedorov’s Election Call Will Fail
content:
The dust was just settling after Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov’s dismissal and the appointment of Yevhenii Khmara as his replacement. Then came the 35-year-old’s extraordinary nine-minute YouTube intervention demanding fresh elections.

If Fedorov was aiming to grab the limelight, he succeeded. But he has not changed the political weather.

The outcome of Ukraine’s political crisis now feels remarkably predictable. Fedorov’s campaign will fail.

Speaking as someone who lives and travels in Ukraine, it is actually quite difficult to find a voter who does not want elections. After more than four years of full-scale war, people naturally hope for democratic renewal, accountability and eventually the opportunity to decide who leads the country into whatever comes next.

But it is even harder to find anyone thinking now is the time for a new vote.

Keep that distinction firmly in mind, because wanting elections and believing they can be held freely, fairly and safely in the middle of this war are two very different things. That’s what made Fedorov’s comments such a surprise; his call seemed badly misjudged.

title: Unbreakable Shield: Why Taiwan’s Chip Expertise Cannot Be Cloned
content:
As Taiwan became the predominant manufacturer of semiconductors, Western governments became frightened and moved to “de-risk” from the vulnerable island that China claims. Taiwan’s leading semiconductor manufacturer TSMC responded by building multi-billion dollar foundries in Arizona, Kyushu, and Dresden. 

But if the goal is to end dependence, the diversification drive is doomed. Taiwan’s semiconductor ecosystem extends far beyond wafer foundries. It includes advanced packaging, materials, substrates, and the dense network of suppliers — all of which remains anchored on the island. Taiwan is no longer a “one-trick pony”; it has become a multi-layer platform almost impossible to replicate.

Consider TSMC’s investment in Arizona. It includes leading-edge fabs producing cutting-edge chips. Yet trade reporting and industry sources note that the technologies required to “package” chips, such as Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate, remain in Taiwan. Packaging lines on the island are fully booked, with long lead times.

title: How AI-Driven Influence Operations Attack Ukraine
content:
When US military aid to Ukraine fell by 99% and Europe stepped into the breach in 2025, Russia’s influence machinery pivoted. Storm-1516, a network linked to the Internet Research Agency, had spent years spreading fabrications aimed at undermining international support for Ukraine. Now it set its sights on the Europeans picking up the tab.

Germany, suddenly Ukraine’s largest military donor at €9bn, and France, whose president had emerged as one of Kyiv’s leading champions, became the primary targets. According to a February 2026 NewsGuard investigation, Storm-1516 has published 34 false claims aimed at the two countries since January 2025, generating 274m views. The core message: Ukraine is bankrupting Europe, exhausting its citizens, and dragging the continent toward war.

title: Wind Blows Strong – Amid Political Turbulence
content:
It was historic. This summer, a cable beneath the Baltic Sea carried the first ever electric  current from an offshore wind farm to the Polish electricity grid. A country long dependent on coal had joined the offshore wind club. 

The timing was revealing. Offshore wind is expanding around the globe, even though the commercial model supporting it has come under strain. The turbines work. Too often, contracts and politics do not.

Global numbers show a wind boom. More than 9.3 gigawatts of offshore wind came online in 2025, taking total capacity to 92.5 gigawatts. Another 50 gigawatts are under construction, and the Global Wind Energy Council expects capacity to reach 420 gigawatts by 2035. 

Yet wind is struggling to keep up with the artificial intelligence buildout that is causing electricity demand to soar. The International Energy Agency expects global data center electricity consumption to roughly double by 2030. US data centers could then consume 9% to 17% of national electricity. At the same time, wind procurement fell in 2025 by 80% from the 2024 record.  Steel is entering the water faster than confidence is entering new contracts.

title: The Coded Resistance of Russian Youth
content:
Russia’s Supreme Court decision to remove the only registered party openly campaigning for peace, Yabloko, from the ballot for September’s State Duma election has revived the question of how many Russians oppose the Kremlin’s war and how much space remains to express that opposition. 

It is certainly a signal of the regime’s resolve. After all, if a Western-style liberalism presents no threat to Putin’s despotic system, why ban opponents?

The answer may be found, in part, in events online and particularly among young people. Within a week of registering for the elections, Yabloko attracted a sudden wave of attention on social media, doubling its key social media metrics, which made it highly likely to exceed 5% support, a level sufficient to clear the electoral threshold and secure seats in parliament.

title: Ukraine’s War After the War
content:
“The war after the war has already begun,” warned Ksana Nechyporenko, co-founder of GoGlobal, an organization that helps young Ukrainians acquire new skills for the 21st century.

Her concern is that when peace does come, the danger to Ukrainian nationhood will not end. Moscow will still retain powerful tools to disrupt and derail a wounded country’s path to a better future. The Kremlin will employ its full armory against Ukraine: everything from disinformation and cyberattacks to political manipulation and economic pressure.

For her, the danger is that Ukraine will emerge exhausted, drained, grieving from the war, and all too vulnerable to manipulation. She expects a vast effort to infiltrate Ukraine’s media and political space, amplifying every possible fracture.

Russia, she warned, is skilled at spotting a topic that can divide a country and then flooding the information space around it. She listed several flashpoints:

  • Those who left the country versus those who stayed
  • Soldiers versus civilians
  • Russian speakers versus Ukrainian speakers
  • Regions against regions
  • Political parties vying for power

    • “You can see Russian footprints everywhere,” she said. “They spend billions sowing dissent.”
snippet: “The war after the war has already begun,” warned Ksana Nechyporenko, co-founder of GoGlobal, an organization that helps young Ukrainians acquire new skills for the 21st century.
creator: Sara George

title: Whisper Music to Our Weary Spirits
content:
These days, geopolitics is everywhere. Just look at soccer’s 2026 World Cup and the fallout that threatens a rift in humanity’s most popular sport. The Eurovision Song Contest, once widely derided as laughably insipid, is now the battlefield for endless disputes about politics. Book festivals have not been spared.

In fact, only one part of international human interaction remains mostly harmonious, and appropriately enough, that’s classical music.

This summer I had a vision. I saw people from all over the world co-exist and cooperate productively and without consideration for anything other than the final product. More precisely, what I saw wasn’t really a vision at all: it was the Verbier Festival, a classical-music extravaganza in the Swiss Alps, where I saw a world that may have seemed normal a couple of decades ago, even one decade ago.

title: Unleashing Private Hackers to Fight Cybercriminals
content:
An Ohio woman received a text message from an unknown number. What followed appeared to be a friendship, built through conversations about hobbies, family, and religion. It was, in fact, the beginning of a cryptocurrency investment scam.

By the time she realized the truth, the scammers had taken approximately $663,000, including her life savings and Roth IRA. When the money ran out, they threatened her family. Her story is one among thousands. The FBI now receives approximately 3,000 complaints per day.

In response to this danger, a national security memorandum authorizes vetted US companies to conduct cyber surveillance and cyber effects operations against foreign criminal organizations. It’s a significant move. Although the concept of unleashing the private sector has long been discussed, previous administrations hesitated, fearful that the move could escalate cyber conflict.

title: AI and Cybersecurity: Same Challenges, Less Time
content:
Artificial intelligence makes it impossible to ignore cybersecurity. The use of advanced AI tools for autonomous hacking leads directly to two of cybersecurity’s most intractable problems: the difficulty of getting the private sector to adopt adequate cybersecurity measures and the reluctance to counter foreign actors who can’t be held unaccountable. These are problems of markets and diplomacy that date back to the 1990s.

Mythos and similar AI tools automate the hacking process, speed up the discovery of vulnerabilities or configuration errors, and write code to exploit them. AI tools exploit software errors and weak cyber defense. Since this is automated, there is increased risk of collateral damage if the tool attacks something other than the intended target. Risks that once seemed acceptable have increased. The vulnerabilities that allow exploitation are not new — the means to exploit them are.

title: Russia’s Nuclear Weapons: Sanctified by God?
content:
August is a month of recollection. For it was then, in 1945, that the United States changed humanity forever by dropping atom bombs on Hiroshima (August 6) and Nagasaki (August 9) and killing up to a quarter million Japanese civilians.

August is also a month of responsibility, when clerics and other religious leaders remind humanity that peace is preferable to war, and that using weapons of mass destruction is intrinsically wrong  — even if it shortens a war.

Policymakers may argue for or against the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons, analysts may debate their ability to deter aggression, and historians can disagree over the strategic utility of destroying Hiroshima and Nagasaki (and of the Anglo-US conventional bombing of Dresden), but the men and women of God really have no alternative to condemning them, even if their condemnations strike some as naive.

Pope Leo XIV, for instance, has noted that “true peace demands the courageous laying down of weapons — especially those with the power to cause an indescribable catastrophe” and that “nuclear arms offend our shared humanity and also betray the dignity of creation.”

title: Russia Makes Hostages of Kherson Civilians
content:
In the Ukrainian city of Kherson, a Russian drone was recently seen hunting a 52 year-old market vendor, chasing him and striking him, leaving him injured. The images were widely shared on social media but the grotesque mistreatment of civilians by the Russian forces is commonplace.

That’s especially the case in Kherson, where Russian forces conduct “human safaris” to forcibly depopulate the area.

Just south of the city, in the occupied zone on the far bank of the River Dnipro, Ukrainians in the shattered frontline city of Oleshky face dire humanitarian conditions. Unable to leave because of Russian controls, as many as 2,000 of the former population of 24,000 still remain. The area was also heavily impacted by Russia’s sabotage of the Nova Kakhovka dam in 2023.

Delivery of basic commercial goods has become rare, local medical care greatly lacking operating with generator power, and no safe passage has been organized for those who wish to leave. Inhabitants are suffering “hellish conditions,” according to a July report from Human Rights Watch.

On the Ukrainian-held bank, including Kherson, around 60,000 civilians endure constant Russian strikes.

title: Ukraine War Bleeds Into the Caspian
content:
According to Iranian authorities, the Ukrainian attack on vessels sailing between Russian and Iranian ports on the Caspian Sea killed one Iranian sailor and injured three others, prompting Tehran to summon Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires and condemn the strike as a “hostile and criminal act.”

It marked Ukraine’s first known attack on an Iranian vessel — it has previously hit Russian targets in and around the sea — and caused Iran’s foreign ministry to describe President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as “the head of the Ukraine regime”. It pledged the late July attacks would be answered. Zelenskyy subsequently confirmed Ukrainian strikes against vessels which he said were transporting Iran-linked military cargo, thus removing any ambiguity regarding Kyiv’s intent. One vessel was traveling from Russia’s Astrakhan to Iran’s port of Anzali.

title: Environmental Justice for Ukraine and Ecocide Deterrence
content:
A panel of international experts drafted a definition of the crime of ecocide in 2021 as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with the knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”

Yet, despite numerous efforts at both national and international levels, including by the Ecocide Law Alliance, most civil-law states lack a crime of ecocide in their criminal codes.

While its criminalization would be complex and politically contentious even in peacetime, armed conflict creates an urgent need to establish legal frameworks for adjudication and accountability for severe environmental harm.

Ukraine has faced significant challenges investigating and prosecuting ecocide since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, and there is little room for delay. Faced with continuous environmental destruction, Kyiv had no choice but to move forward with investigations and charges as the war continued.
